title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
In this lab we will begin to build the foundation for working withmeasurement
uncertainty. Before learning formal methods, it is essential to practice concepts
such asestimation,bounding, andorder-of-magnitude reasoning. Especially when it is
useful in situations where quantities cannot be measured directly. These skills help us
decide whether a result is reasonable and how reliable it might be.
These skills form the first step toward a systematic treatment of uncertainty, which
you will develop further in later labs. These first steps mirror how scientists approach
real problems: starting with rough estimates, bounding possibilities, and then refining
to quantified uncertainties.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
Although science is rooted in precise measurement, scientists and engineers often begin
with approximate estimates. These serve as a ‘sanity check’—a way to anticipate
results, choose appropriate instruments, and identify mistakes early (e.g., wrong units
or unrealistic values). This exercise about how to move confidently between rough
intuition and systematic measurement.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
In many experiments, you will face situations where quantities cannot be measured
immediately or directly. In these cases, it is valuable to begin with anestimate—a
reasoned approximation of the result you expect. Estimation helps you decide what
instruments or methods are appropriate and provides a reference point against which
later measurements can be compared.
What matters most is not whether your estimate is exact, but whether you have a
clear idea of how far off itcouldbe. Even a rough estimate can be very useful when it
helps you detect mistakes, choose equipment, or check the plausibility of results.
Mini rule-of-thumb:Estimates within a factor of 2–3 are typical of reasonable
human judgment. A difference of a full order of magnitude (a factor of 10) often
signals a unit error or faulty reasoning.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
A natural companion to estimation isbounding. Bounding a quantity means identi-
fying values that itcannotreasonably exceed or fall below. Anupper boundis a
value greater than the true result, while alower boundis a value smaller than the
true result. Together, these bounds form a safe “bracket” around the unknown value.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.2 Bounding > 3.2.1 Picking Realistic Bounds
text:
Reasonable bounds can often be set by comparison with known quantities. For
example:
• To estimate a person’s height, you might compare them with friends or family
members of known height. A taller person gives an upper bound; a shorter
person gives a lower bound.
• To estimate the mass of an unfamiliar object, you can compare it to objects you
know well. Something clearly heavier provides an upper bound, while something
lighter provides a lower bound. Wide bounds are safe but not useful. Narrower
bounds make your estimate more powerful.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
When the unknown quantity is similar to something you already know, comparison is
one of the most effective tools for estimation. If you can bracket the unknown value
between a higher and a lower bound, you can usually place your estimate somewhere
in between with reasonable confidence.
For example, if you know the mass of one object is smaller than your upper bound
and larger than your lower bound, then your estimate should reflect a value between
those two reference points.

section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.3 Familiar Comparisons > 3.3.1 Illustration of Comparison
text:
To illustrate, we’ll try to make a few simple estimates. The first question we want to
answer is:
IQ1:How tall is your TA?
1. Identify a person who is shorter than the IA (this person can be one of your
group members or a celebrity). Record that person’s height. This quantity is a
lower bound for the IA’s height.
2. Identify a person who is taller than the IA (this person can be one of your group
members or a celebrity). Record that person’s height. This quantity is an upper
bound for the IA’s height.
3. Estimate the IA’s height according to the two known heights and explain your
reasoning.
4. Adjust the bounds you would place on the IA’s height so that there is a smaller
range of values. Are these bounds the same as a) and b)? If not, explain how
you adjusted (and estimated) the bounds. (i.e. if you saw someone about his/her
height commit a crime, what range of heights would you give to investigators so
that it would be of use in identifying suspects? The range of values has to be
very small for it to be of good use!!!)
The goal when making estimates is to try and make them “safe” but “useful”; i.e.
you arepretty sureabout lower and upper bounds on your estimate, but the bounds
need to be close enough together to make the estimate usable.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.4 Less Familiar Comparison
text:
In some cases, it is not easy to find a familiar object to compare with the quantity of
interest. When there is nothing clearly similar, your estimate will naturally become
less precise and the bounds you choose will be more uncertain.
For example, it is difficult to set upper and lower bounds for the height of the Eiffel
Tower. Unlike comparing a person’s height to family or friends, there is no everyday
reference object that is truly comparable. In such situations, estimates and bounds
must be broader and more approximate, yet they are still useful.

•the mass of a laboratory table (in kilograms)
(Please do not attempt to lift the table!)

section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations
text:
In physics labs,order of magnitude (OM)calculations are often done early, using
preliminary or estimated data, to check whether results seem reasonable. They serve
Figure 1: Conrad Hall, for comparison
as a quick “sanity check” before spending time on precise measurements.
Order of magnitude refers to thepower of tenthat best describes a quantity. Raising
a number by one order of magnitude multiplies it by 10; lowering it divides it by 10.
For example:
•200 and 600 are the same order of magnitude (hundreds, or102).
•0.02 is one order of magnitude smaller than 0.2.
• A city with 1,000,000 people (106) is three orders of magnitude larger than a
town of 1,000 people (103).
Since an order of magnitude calculation is intended to be “within a factor of ten,” you
should be reasonably confident that:
•Ten times your value is clearly too large,
•One-tenth of your value is clearly too small.

Why Order of Magnitude Matters
• Error detection:Using the wrong unit (e.g., cm instead of m) will often shift
your result by several orders of magnitude, making the mistake obvious.
• Quick checks:Scientists use OM reasoning to judge whether a result is
physically realistic.
• Decision making:OM estimates guide choices of instrument sensitivity or
experimental method.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations > 3.5.1 Example: How many gold parking spaces are there at Laurier?
text:
Estimation problems in science often ask us to reason from limited data. The goal is
not to get an exact number but to reach a reasonableorder-of-magnitudeestimate.
Let us try this with the number ofgold parking spaces(faculty and staff only) on
campus.
1. Gold lots are reserved for faculty and staff, so the number of spots must be
smaller than the total number of employees at Laurier, since many walk, take
the bus, or carpool.
2. There are several lots of different sizes. A good strategy is to estimate the
average size of a lot and multiply by the number of lots.
From observation:
• The lot in front of the Science Building has about 50 spaces (roughly 25 per
side).
•Suppose there are about 10 similar lots across campus.
IfSis the average number of spaces per lot andLis the number of lots, then
N=S×L
so withS≈50andL≈10,
N≈50×10 = 500.
Does this make sense?
•More than 50?Yes—since one lot already has about 50.
• Less than 5000?Laurier has about 10,000 students. For 5000 gold spots to exist,
there would need to be one faculty or staff member for every two students. In
reality, the ratio is closer to 1 staff for every 10 students, so 5000 is much too
high.
Thus, an estimate of about500 gold spotsis reasonable.
One of the important features of order-of-magnitude reasoning is that it is often
self-correcting: you may overestimate some parts and underestimate others, but the
errors tend to balance out, leaving you close to the right order of magnitude.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations > 3.5.2 Illustration of Order of Magnitude Calculation
text:
Any time you use anestimatedquantity in a calculation, you are performing anorder
of magnitude (OM) calculation. The purpose is not to obtain an exact answer,
but to check whether the result falls in a reasonable range.
Theorder of magnitudeof a quantity refers to the power of ten that best describes it.
For example:
• The height of a typical building might be written as∼ 101 metres (tens of
metres).
•The length of an entire campus might be∼102 metres (hundreds of metres).
Thus, saying that the length of the Science Building is
•“about 100 metres,” or
•“between 50 and 200 metres,”
are both acceptable order-of-magnitude estimates. What matters is that the result
lands in the correctballpark.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations > 3.5.3 When are Order of Magnitude Calculations used?
text:
Order of magnitude reasoning is common in science and engineering:
• Before experiments:to anticipate what range of values to expect, and to
decide which instruments or methods are suitable.
• During data collection:to check whether preliminary results make sense in
real time.
• Afterward:to identify errors, such as unit mistakes, which often shift results
by entire orders of magnitude.
Key idea:Any calculation involving at least one estimated quantity is an order-of-

tells us how confident we are about a measured or estimated value, expressed as a
central value± some range. Instead of always writing separate lower and upper
bounds, we compress this information into a single statement.

upper boundU, a practical estimate and uncertainty are:

estimation.
• Error= the actual difference between a measured value and the true value
(unknown in most real experiments).
Even if your value equals a “known” reference, you must still report an uncertainty.
Because uncertainty reflects how the value was obtained, not how close it happens
to be.

section: Appendix A: Reference Material > A.1 Significant Figures (SigFigs)
text:
Why they matter.Significant figures reflect the precision of a measurement and
keep reported results consistent with the quality of the data.
Core rules
•All nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 123.4 has 4 sig figs).
•Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 1002 has 4 sig figs).
•Leading zeros arenotsignificant (e.g., 0.00450 has 3 sig figs).
• Trailing zeros are significantifa decimal point is present (e.g., 45.00 has 4 sig
figs; 4500 has 2 sig figs unless written as4.500×103).
Operations
• Multiplication/Division:keep the same number of sig figs as the factor with
the fewest sig figs.
Example:(2.6cm)×(3.14cm) = 8.164cm 2→8.16cm 2 (3 sig figs).
•Addition/Subtraction:round to the least precisedecimal place.
Example:12.30 + 0.456 = 12.756→12.76(hundredths place).
Worked exampleYou measure a block’s edges as12.3cm,3 .40cm, and0 .85cm.
Volume:
V= (12.3)(3.40)(0.85) = 35.511cm 3 →35.5cm 3
(3 sig figs overall; the limiting factor is 0.85 with 2 sig figs? No—0.85 hastwosig figs,
so strictly you should report35cm3. If your instrument actually supportsthreesig
figs for each edge, keep 3 sig figs. Match this to your instrument’s markings.)
Common pitfallWriting 4500 without context is ambiguous. Prefer4 .5× 103 (2
sig figs),4.50×10 3 (3), or4.500×10 3 (4).

title: PC141 Tutorial Announcements (MyLS)
text:
The tutorial component is held every week and is designed to support students in
developing strong conceptual understanding, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills
in physics.
Tutorials provide a structured and supportive environment in which students actively
engage with physics problems related to the course material. Each session focuses on
reasoning, application, and analysis, rather than passive review.
During tutorials, we work through carefully selected problems together. Students receive
real-time guidance and feedback, encouraging them to:
• Think critically about physical situations in a variety of contexts
• Apply physics concepts with increasing confidence
• Refine the accuracy, clarity, and coherence of the reasoning
This iterative, hands-on problem-solving process strengthens conceptual foundations and
cultivates a methodical scientific mindset—skills essential for success in both academic
studies and professional scientific or technical fields.
